item.title: Suspected crime boss Daniel Kinahan appears in court after extradition
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c62qd5plzp6o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Suspected crime boss Daniel Kinahan appears in court after extradition - Published Suspected crime boss Daniel Kinahan, one of the world's most wanted men, has appeared before a Dublin court after being extradited from Dubai. He has been charged with directing the activities of a criminal organisation between 18 October 2015 and 6 April 2017. An Irish government jet carrying the 49-year-old landed in Dublin after 18:00 local time. He was arrested and charged upon his arrival. Following a 13-minute non-jury hearing at the Special Criminal Court, he was remanded in custody until 5 October. Kinahan was arrested in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) in April. He appealed the extradition order over the past few months but his attempts were unsuccessful. The National Crime Agency (NCA) has previously said that the Kinahan cartel has been responsible for importing tonnes of drugs and firearms around the world and has also been linked to more than a dozen gangland murders. Kinahan was not only wanted by the authorities in Ireland - the US Treasury Department once described the Kinahan cartel as one of the most dangerous in the world. The US government imposed sanctions on Kinahan in April 2022 after identifying him and other member of his family as leaders of the Kinahan organised crime cartel. He fought attempts to extradite him back to his native country, where the Kinahan cartel was involved in a long-running gangland feud that claimed 18 lives. A large-scale security operation was in place ahead of Sunday's hearing. Ahead of the extradition, the Irish Prison Service bought a bulletproof and bombproof van which can be used to escort prisoners who are considered high-risk. Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly said the arrest shows the force's determination to "target transnational organised crime groups" alongside international policing partners such as Dubai police. He added it shows the value of the force's relationship with the authorities in the UAE, the Irish ministry of justice at judicial level, and "on a police-to-police basis". 'I won't be getting bail' Kinahan arrived at Baldonnell Casement Aerodrome on Sunday evening, where gardaí arrested and charged him. He was directly transported under heavy police guard to the Criminal Courts of Justice in Dublin. All the benches were full in a packed courtroom of journalists, a number of solicitors from the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP), some members of the public and court clerks. In court, Kinahan was sitting on a wooden bench and wearing a black hooded top. He appeared before judges Patrick McGrath, Sarah Berkeley and Fiona Lydon, and rose to his feet when the three judges took their places. Kinahan did not have legal representation, and told the court that he did not have time to arrange this. When Judge McGrath suggested that he should be charged today and legal representation arranged later on, Kinahan replied: "If I have time, yes." Det Sgt Colm Davison told the court he arrested Kinahan earlier that evening. Judge McGrath asked Kinahan if he would like to appear at the next court sitting in person or via videolink. Kinahan asked if he had to "decide now" and it was explained to him he could make a decision later and notify the governor in the prison. Judge McGrath explained to Kinahan he could file an application for bail through the High Court. Kinahan replied: "I think we all know I won't be getting bail, but thank you for your time." 'Landmark of judicial cooperation' The UAE and Ireland have an extradition treaty and on Sunday justice ministers from both jurisdictions issued a joint statement welcoming Kinahan's extradition. "The Irish national is regarded as one of the most high-profile individuals sought for prosecution in connection with transnational organised crime and is accused of directing an organised crime organisation," it stated. Irish Justice Minister Jim O'Callaghan described the extradition as a "landmark of judicial cooperation between the two countries". He also commended "the professionalism, efficiency, and diligence demonstrated by the UAE judicial authorities throughout the extradition proceedings". His UAE counterpart, Abdullah bin Sultan bin Awad Al Nuaimi, said it underscored "the steadfast commitment we have to supporting global efforts to combat transnational organised crime". The extradition agreement was previously used to extradite Sean McGovern, a "senior lieutenant" in the Kinahan organised crime group. He was sentenced to 24 years in prison in June for directing the activities of a criminal organisation. What is the Kinahan cartel? According to former Garda Commissioner Drew Harris, the gang is estimated to have made more than €1bn (£857,870,000) globally from its activities. The US Treasury Department has in the past compared the gang to crime organisations such as Italy's Camorra, Mexico's Los Zetas and Japan's Yakuza. A reward of up to $5m (£3.7m) has also been offered by the US for information on Daniel, his father Christopher Snr and brother Christopher Jnr. In 2022, Thomas Kavanagh, who the NCA said ran the group's criminal operations in the UK, was jailed for 21 years alongside Gary Vickery and Daniel Canning, who were sentenced to 20 years and 19 and a half years respectively. The NCA said evidence showed they were responsible for cocaine imports estimated to be up to £23.4m, and cannabis imports worth about £6.4m. Kinahan himself became a target for murder and escaped an attempt on his life during a fatal shooting at a Dublin hotel in 2016. He left Ireland and spent time living in Spain and more recently in Dubai, where a warrant for his arrest was issued by the Irish courts in April. Daniel Kinahan's lawyer previously told BBC Panorama that he has no criminal record or convictions and allegations about him being a crime boss are false and have no evidential basis.

item.title: Israel rejects Trump's 15-point plan for Gaza, Netanyahu says
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5yw4lpe0yeo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Israel rejects Trump's 15-point plan for Gaza, Netanyahu says - Published Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected US President Donald Trump's 15-point plan for Gaza, stating that no military pull-out will happen until Hamas is "genuinely" disarmed. Trump's Board of Peace said last month it had reached an agreement for the "complete disarmament" of Hamas and other armed groups in Gaza. But Hamas said handing over its heavy weapons was contingent on Israel ending "all forms of aggression" and withdrawing its forces from Gaza. Israel has continued to carry out strikes on Gaza since agreeing to an initial ceasefire in the territory last October. "Israel rejects the 15-point document," Netanyahu said at a cabinet meeting on Sunday. The Israeli military "will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and our citizens", he added. A Hamas official told the BBC on Sunday the group "reaffirms it commitment" to the agreement and it was ready "to engage seriously and responsibly in implementing" the 15-point plan. They called on mediators to ensure "that all parties comply with what has been agreed". Israel's rejection signals another blow for Trump's Gaza peace plan which was announced in September last year. The plan included the creation of the Board of Peace to oversee the agreement's implementation, as well as the disarmament of Hamas, withdrawal of Israeli troops and reconstruction of Gaza. - What's in the Gaza peace deal roadmap? - Published31 July Netanyahu's statement does not come as a surprise. But he has taken some time to make it, perhaps reflecting the difficult position the Israeli leader is in. He clearly is unhappy with Trump's plan but at the same time he will not want to upset his closest ally. It's just over a week since Trump announced what he called a "monumental step toward lasting peace and security" - that Hamas for the first time had agreed to disarm, on condition that Israel withdraws its forces from Gaza. On Sunday, Netanyahu was clear that was not going to happen under his watch. He said Hamas had to disarm first, adding that it couldn't be some "fictitious disarmament" - it had to be real. The reality is any disarmament and withdrawal of Israeli forces would likely need to be phased. Netanyahu said he was now in discussion with US officials about how to go forward. "They have ideas; some of them are acceptable to us and some are not, and we know how to stand our ground on these matters," he said. But just months before Israeli elections and under pressure from members of his right-wing coalition to take a tough stance on Gaza, he is unlikely to want to make concessions. He has faced calls from far-right parts of the coalition to hold a new cabinet vote and end the Gaza plan, including National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir who dismissed the draft as "not acceptable". Nickolay Mladenov - a senior diplomat tasked with implementing Donald Trump's peace plan - defended the plan on Sunday and said discussions were ongoing in the hope of a "positive outcome". The board's high representative for Gaza told Israel's Channel 12 that Israel had been asked "to give the process a chance" and said the plan was "the only way forward" to ensure there was no repeat of the 7 October 2023 attack by Hamas. Mladenov said the plan was built on a process that was "verifiable, that is reversible, that at each stage can be stopped, and that we have built up with a very clear-eyed understanding of what are the challenges ahead". He also said that Israel would not be required to withdraw until it could be verified that Hamas was taking steps to disarm. According to the United Nations, about 1.9 million people - 90% of Gaza's population - have been displaced in the territory since the war in Gaza started. The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage. Israel responded to the attack by launching a military campaign in Gaza, during which more than 73,000 people have been killed, according to the territory's health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations. item.title: Evidence that South African special forces murdered top detective shared with BBC
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cly8djwgem0o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Evidence that South African special forces murdered top detective shared with BBC - Published Senior police detective Frans Mathipa had been fighting for four months to gain access to a crucial piece of information in the case he was working on. Finally, he was told, it was going to come his way. But he feared his pursuit of it could cost him his life. Two days later, his car was found overturned - he had been shot dead while driving. Now seven members of South Africa's special forces, and one military police officer, have been charged with murdering Lt Col Mathipa, a highly respected officer, in August 2023. They deny the charges. There has been no date scheduled for their trial, and there are concerns it will never go ahead, because three of the men charged with his murder have refused to comply with a court order revoking their bail. They are still working for the army's special forces, and one of them has been promoted. The BBC World Service has been given exclusive access to the prosecution case against all the men. The case has caused consternation in one of Africa's most robust democracies, with fears the country's military is significantly overreaching its mandate. We asked the South African army whether it was responsible for Mathipa's killing. It did not respond. Several hundred pages of secret police and court documents, shared with the BBC, set out the evidence suggesting special forces killed Mathipa - who worked for an elite police unit known as "The Hawks". We have also interviewed key sources in the police investigation - South Africa's former head of counter-terrorism in The Hawks; Mathipa's commanding officer; and Mathipa's family - to build the most comprehensive public account of the events leading up to the detective's death. It presents a compelling case that South Africa's special forces are responsible for his murder. In particular, police documents show that the vehicle that trailed Mathipa just before he was shot was registered to a front company for the special forces. And that tracking data found in that vehicle puts it at the scene of the shooting. One of the men in the car, Maj Sunnybooi Wambi, the documents show, was also spotted at the scene of an alleged abduction carried out by special forces soldiers - the case that Mathipa had been investigating. After Mathipa's death, special forces issued a chilling warning to The Hawks, the police documents say. "You can appoint 10 investigating officers; we will kill all of them," said the warning, according to police. South Africa: Anatomy of a cover-up Africa Eye uncovers a disturbing story of power, secrecy and murder. Watch on iPlayer - or listen on BBC Sounds to the podcast, Special forces on trial Special forces on trial - episode two available from 24 August. The case Mathipa had been investigating was sensitive. It centred on an Ethiopian man called Abdella Abadigga, an alleged so-called Islamic State [IS] militant. He had been granted temporary asylum in South Africa in 2008, but was arrested abroad in 2017. Abadigga had then been smuggled back into the country, by the South African military and Department of Home Affairs, to be used as an intelligence asset - but had "gone rogue", according to Col Tollie Vreugdenburg, former head of counter-terrorism in The Hawks. Abadigga had gone on to extort Johannesburg's Ethiopian neighbourhood, sources in the community told us. This money was used to fund IS, says the US government. We asked the South African army if it had facilitated Abadigga's return to South Africa. And we asked the Department of Home Affairs if it had lied about a planned deportation of him to Ethiopia, and had instead smuggled him back into South Africa on an expired passport and refugee permit. They did not respond. Specifically, Mathipa was investigating the allegation that special forces had then gone on to abduct and kill Abadigga in December 2022 - who the United States, earlier that year, had put under sanctions, designating him an IS recruiter and fundraiser, as well as a trusted supporter of Bilal al-Sudani, a top IS figure in Somalia. Court documents show that after Abadigga's abduction, his phone connected to a mast near a military base. Police sources say it was used to call a number in Somalia. The Pentagon did not respond to the BBC's question on whether Abadigga's phone helped locate al-Sudani, who was killed by US special forces in Somalia in January 2023, only a few weeks after Abadigga's alleged abduction. We also asked South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa whether Abadigga had been kidnapped at the behest of the US. He declined to comment. When Mathipa was assigned the case, four months before his own death, he already knew special forces were implicated, but he was trying to secure more evidence. He was building on information already gathered by Abadigga's brother, Ameen - who had opened a missing person's case soon after the disappearance, and had been assigned an investigating officer (IO) from local police. He and the IO had obtained CCTV footage showing the last known movements of Abadigga and his bodyguard Kadir Abotese at the Mall of Africa, a shopping centre on the outskirts of Johannesburg. The footage, clips of which the BBC has seen, shows a man in a blue top following Abadigga and his bodyguard as they leave the food court to head back to the car park, and paying for parking three seconds after Abadigga and Abotese do. The mall CCTV footage contains another vital clue. The licence plates of the suspected kidnappers' vehicles are clearly visible. The vehicles were all registered to a company called Peters Communications Trust (PCT), a front company for South African special forces - Ameen and the IO were to discover. At the time of Abadigga's disappearance, PCT's directors included Maj Gen Herbert Mashego, the then commanding officer of 5 Special Forces Regiment. Police documents say a meeting was arranged between the IO and high ranks of the military, including Brig Gen Yalo, the then head of special forces, at which the IO was instructed to tell Ameen there was no link between PCT and the military. So, with the investigation seemingly at a standstill, Abadigga's brother took his case to the Johannesburg High Court. Responding to Ameen's legal action, special forces denied all knowledge of Abadigga or his whereabouts. They did, however, admit their soldiers had been at the Mall of Africa on the date in question, but said they had been there for a training exercise. They named the man seen wearing blue on CCTV as Maj Sunnybooi Wambi, and said he had been the exercise commander. They also admitted all the suspect vehicles seen at the mall belonged to them. Domestic operations by South Africa's military need to be authorised by both the government and the presidency. We asked South African former Defence Minister Thandi Modise, and President Ramaphosa, if they had authorised a training exercise in the Mall of Africa - Modise did not respond and Ramaphosa declined to comment. When Mathipa was assigned to the case a month later, he issued a subpoena to special forces to force them to hand over full details of this alleged training exercise and all the personnel involved. When access to these documents was finally promised, three months later, Mathipa had a premonition that he would be murdered - according to Brig Paulina Sekgobela, his commanding officer. "When [Mathipa] left my office he said: 'Brigadier, you know, these people - they are going to kill me. I'm going to die'," she told the BBC. On the day Mathipa was killed, he was phoned by a man calling himself Tebogo, who claimed he had information on the case for the detective - according to Mathipa's daughter Basetsana, who was home with him at the time. Mathipa and Tebogo arranged to meet at a petrol station in Pretoria. When Tebogo failed to show, Mathipa drove away again, along the highway. He was killed while driving, by rounds fired from high-velocity weapons which special forces would have had access to, according to South African police. And footage from motorway toll gantries, police say, shows one of the occupants of the black BMW, which tailed Mathipa moments before his murder, was Maj Sunnybooi Wambi. This car, like the three vehicles connected with Abadigga's disappearance at the mall, was registered to PCT, they add. New detectives were assigned to the case after Mathipa's death, triggering a chilling message from special forces, that made its way to the police's Criminal Intelligence division. Police say it warned that, however many investigating officers were assigned to the case, "we will kill all of them". Twelve members of the South African military have been arrested in total, including Lt Col Sunnybooi Wambi, and the current head of South Africa's special forces, Brig Gen Solomon Lechoenyo - both promoted to these positions since police first started investigating their roles in the case. The 12 have been variously charged with the abduction and murder of Abadigga and Abotese, the murder of Mathipa, fraud, and obstruction. All deny all charges and they were initially released on bail. But six of them later had their bail revoked, and were ordered to turn themselves in to custody. Three of the six, including Wambi, have been charged with both Mathipa's murder, and Abotese's abduction and murder. The military has refused to hand them over. In July, their lawyers cited mental health treatment for their absence. Three years after Mathipa's killing, no trial date has been set. Meanwhile, Abadigga's body has never been found. "[Mathipa] was barking up the right tree. He was taking on the right lion," Vreugdenburg says of the late detective. Mathipa's daughter Basetsana puts it starkly: "We need justice. I'm never going to see my dad anymore... Why my dad? Because he was doing his job."

item.title: Drones spotted over German base days after Leipzig bomb incident
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwyeg1ljp2eo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Drones spotted over German base days after Leipzig bomb incident - Published Two drones were spotted over a military base in western Germany just days after an explosive-laden device was found at Leipzig airport. Germany's armed forces (Bundeswehr) confirmed they were seen on Thursday evening at a base in Mechernich, near Bonn, reportedly housing components for US-made Patriot air-defence systems. A spokeswoman for the Bundeswehr Joint Force Command said military police were deployed to the site before the matter was handed over to local police. It is the latest instance of drones being spotted near military bases or airports in European nations supporting Ukraine in its war with Russia, on which suspicion has fallen. Moscow has consistently denied any involvement. German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told newspaper Bild on Sunday that Germany had become a regular target of "destabilising" attacks. "We're not at war, but we are the daily target of hybrid warfare," he said. Germany is currently investigating how a drone laden with explosives was able to reach a runway at Leipzig/Halle airport, which is used by Nato, the Germany military and serves as a base for Ukraine's Antonov Airlines. The Bundeswehr declined to comment on the ongoing investigation when asked by the BBC on Sunday about the suspected origins of the drones spotted above Mechernich. The local police force has been contacted for comment. German media reports that the base has a storage facility for equipment and spare parts used to maintain the Patriot missile batteries. The air-defence systems have become crucial to Ukraine's ability to intercept Russian ballistic missiles since Moscow's full-scale invasion began in 2022. However, President Volodymyr Zelensky this week pleaded to allies for further supplies, warning that Ukraine was running out of interceptor missiles. After initially offering Ukraine license to make Patriots in early July, US President Donald Trump last week denied any such agreement. A spate of drone sightings in European airspace last year left the continent on high alert, prompting the EU to discuss a continent-wide "drone wall" of air defences. Some European officials have blamed Russia for these drone sightings, claims Moscow has previously described as "absurd". - Published4 days ago - Published2 days ago - Published25 September 2025

item.title: Ancient Roman shipwreck discovered off Sicily coast
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgx1kpz17go?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Ancient Roman shipwreck discovered off Sicily coast - Published Italian divers have discovered an ancient Roman shipwreck off the coast of Sicily, believed to be more than 2,000 years old. The vessel was found piled high with hundreds of well-preserved containers, which were used to transport goods such as wine and olive oil. Italy's Culture Minister Alessandro Giuli hailed the wreck as "one of the most important underwater archaeological discoveries of recent years". Specialist police divers found the ship around 46m (150ft) deep, after a tip-off from fishermen. The wreckage is 21m (69ft) long and 6m (20ft) wide, according to reports in local media. The culture ministry says it dates from the second or 1st Century BC. Fisherman and free-diver Giacomo De Mola described stumbling across the historic vessel while surveying the seabed near Mazara del Vallo. He wrote on social media that he had decided to dive and investigate after seeing something that appeared to be a large rock on his scanner. "I get closer. And my heart stops. It wasn't a rock," he said. Instead, he saw hundreds of amphorae - tall ceramic jars used to store goods in the ancient era, mostly wine, oil or grain. "This is, without a doubt, the most incredible discovery of my life," he said. "It's hard to describe what it feels like to be among the first humans, in nearly 20 centuries, to see that place again." He posted a video of the wreck, showing eels, snappers and "countless marine life" living among the jars, noting: "The sea never ceases to amaze us. "This time we didn't just find a wreck, we found a piece of our history." Specialist divers from the cultural heritage protection arm of Italy's police, known as the Carabinieri Art Squad, were sent to the site. Officials say safety measures will be taken to safeguard it while it undergoes investigation, as experts work to determine the nature of the wreck and learn more about its cargo. The Mediterranean seabed is thought to be scattered with similar ancient wrecks. Another 1st or 2nd Century BC vessel was found north-west of Rome in 2023, again laden with hundreds of amphorae. In 2018, a Greek merchant ship dating back more than 2,400 years was found lying on its side off the Bulgarian coast. At the time, it was hailed as the world's oldest-known intact shipwreck. item.title: Residents warned to brace for the worst as Canada wildfire rages out of control
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx25dkwk3e3o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Residents warned to brace for the worst as Canada wildfire rages out of control - Published A state of emergency has been declared after thousands of people were forced to flee their homes as a fast-moving wildfire spread rapidly in western Canada, doubling in size since it was first detected on Friday. The Bald Range fire now occupies more than 53 sq miles (136 sq km) across Summerland, Peachland and other areas of British Columbia, according to the BC Wildfire Service. "We have to brace ourselves for the worst," Summerland Mayor Doug Holmes told Reuters. The entire Summerland area has been forced to evacuate along with thousands of others in nearby communities. Officials said the flames were so high that they had created their own weather systems, which creates lightning. Keegan Radomski who lives in Summerland said she evacuated her home just moments before the fire reached her property. In a video she shared with the BBC, burning tree tops are seen just over the hill beyond the road where Radomski made her escape. "This is right by our house," she said in the video, her voice trembling. Radomski said she has been unable to return since she fled with seven others on Friday. Now they're anxiously waiting on word whether they will still have a home to return to. She said some neighbours who stayed behind have reported many homes on their street burned down. "There are homes that have been confirmed gone, and a lot are in the area near our home. So, we're pretty scared," she said. "The uncertainty is scary." Residents that spoke to the BBC described the wildfire as one that intensified dramatically with little warning before it reached its current size of 13,618 hectares, external (33,650 acres). British Columbia Premier David Eby told a news conference on Saturday that one fire official had likened the fire to "a bomb going off". "Homes have been lost, and properties have been destroyed. Some people became trapped as conditions changed very quickly, and needed to be rescued," the premier said. A state of emergency allows the provincial government access to special powers including travel restrictions and supply protections to prevent price gouging, and extra resources to coordinate rescue work. Summerland, which has a population of about 12,000 people, has been one of the hardest hit areas and forced to evacuate. So were residents in parts of Peachland, which is home to about 6,500 residents. "We have been on evacuation alert many times," said Earl Kurz, a Peachland resident of 30 years. "This is the first time we were actually evacuated." Kurz was on a boat with his wife in Okanagan Lake on Friday afternoon, when he saw clear blue skies rapidly turn hazy grey. By nightfall, dark clouds of smoke above a raging wildfire came into view. It was headed towards Kurz. "We watched it from the lake," he said. "It was unreal." Hours later, police knocked on his door and ordered him and his wife to evacuate. Kurz said they are now safe in a camper miles away. The Bald Range wildfires triggered the largest evacuation event this summer and more than 20,000 people across British Columbia have evacuated their homes, officials say. "A lot of farms have been affected. We don't know how many structures have been lost. They're still busy fighting the fire," Summerland Mayor Doug Holmes said. Hundreds of residents living in Summerland care facilities, including senior housing, were being relocated to safer areas, according to Interior Health, a publicly funded health authority in BC. It was not yet clear how many structures had been destroyed in the blaze. The regional districts of Central Okanagan and Okanagan-Similkameen, as well as Snpink'tn Indian Band and the districts of Summerland and Peachland have issued evacuation orders, with evacuation alerts in some areas, according wildfire officials. In Okanagan, there are a lot of horses that residents have been struggling to evacuate, Canadian broadcaster CBC reported. Those unable to relocate their animals left their gates open in the hope the animals would find their own way to safety, local residents told CBC. Some owners also painted markings on their animals to make them easier to identify later, according to the outlet. Hundreds of wildfires have raged across Canada this summer, with nearly 200 burning in Ontario in July, sending air quality in Toronto to one of the worst levels in the world for a few days. Smoke from those Canadian wildfires drifted down into parts of the US, including Minnesota and New York, leading US President Donald Trump to threaten new tariffs on the US's northern neighbour. item.title: Ecuador charges ex-minister over presidential candidate assassination case
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cgjeznj6979o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Ecuador charges ex-minister over presidential candidate assassination case - Published Prosecutors in Ecuador have charged a former interior minister and six others on suspicion of being involved in the assassination of a presidential candidate in 2023. José Serrano and the head of cartel Los Lobos, Wilmer "Pipo" Chavarria, were implicated in the murder of Fernando Villavicencio at a campaign event in the capital, Quito, days before the election. Five people linked to the criminal gang were jailed over the hit in 2024, while Pipo was captured in Spain last year, having faked his own death. Villavicencio, a journalist turned prominent legislator, was known for his anti-corruption stance and was one of few candidates to allege links between organised crime and government officials. He had continued to appear at public campaigns after being given a security detail due to his receiving a number of death threats. Daniel Noboa, who ultimately went on to win the election and become Ecuador's president, has taken a hardline military approach to combatting crime gangs. The five convicted over Villavicencio's murder in 2024 were said to have orchestrated the hit. The alleged gunman was shot dead at the scene, while six other men were found murdered in prison while awaiting trial. The seven named by the Ecuadorean Attorney General's Office on Saturday were accused of playing an indirect role in the killing - many of whom had links to Los Lobos, or "The Wolves", one of the nation's most powerful criminal gangs. Five of these were now considered fugitives, it said. Serrano and Xavier Jordán were currently located in the US, former assemblyman Ronny Aleaga was in Venezuela, while Pipo remained in Spain with an extradition request pending. The Attorney General's Office has requested Interpol red notices for their capture and extradition. Ángel Esteban Aguilar, also known as Lobo Menor, was arrested in Mexico City in March and returned to Ecuador after a red notice was issued over the murder of Villavicencio. He was sentenced to 20 years in prison in 2013 for the murder of Serrano's brother but fled after being granted parole. The other accused is senior Los Lobos member Luis Arboleda. Pre-trial hearings are currently taking place and a judge will decide whether prosecutors have a case that can proceed to a full trial. Ecuador's location - sandwiched between Colombia and Peru, the world's largest producers of cocaine - has turned it into a key transit country for the illicit drug, with cartels like Los Lobos using corruption and violence to control supply routes. It is said to have deep connections to the powerful Jalisco New Generation Cartel in Mexico. Related topics - Published16 November 2025 - Published13 July 2024 - Published10 August 2023

item.title: Nigerian army says it safely rescued 33 people kidnapped by gunmen
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c89nkkvx2veo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Nigerian army says it safely rescued 33 people kidnapped by gunmen - Published Nigeria's army has said it safely rescued 33 people after they were kidnapped by armed men while travelling through the country's north-western Zamfara state. The army said its troops mobilised alongside the police immediately after hearing about the abduction, in the Tsafe area of Zamfara on Saturday afternoon. The military found the kidnappers in the process of moving the hostages to an unknown location, the army said, and the gunmen fled into the nearby bush after coming under fire. Kidnappings by armed groups who hold people for ransom are common in parts of north-western Nigeria and major roads have become targets for attacks. Analysts say ransom payments by desperate families, intermediaries or, in some cases, Nigerian authorities have fuelled the abductions. Nigerian army spokesman Lt-Col Aliyu Danja said it was unclear where the abductors were moving their hostages when troops intercepted them, adding that the army was now attempting to track the kidnappers. "The troops engaged the terrorists with effective fire, forcing them to abandon the victims and flee into adjoining bushes," he said, noting that all the hostages had been recovered without any casualties. Danja warned members of the public in the region to remain vigilant and pass on relevant information to security forces. Nigeria's security forces have recorded a recent success in rescuing kidnapped victims. On Thursday, the country's presidency said that more than 300 people abducted in separate attacks in Nigeria had been rescued. Those freed included 163 people abducted in an attack in February on the Woro and Nuku communities in Kwara state, where scores were killed. At least 145 others had been taken in Niger state. The rescue came weeks after 44 pupils and teachers abducted during a raid on a school in Oyo state were freed after more than 50 days in captivity. Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu said on Wednesday that soldiers would get a pay increase of up to 80% for the government's "deep appreciation" of those battling the nation's enormous security threats. Tinubu is attempting to curb widespread banditry, kidnappings and violence from various armed groups, including Islamist militants. Continuing insecurity nationwide has become a major political issue ahead of the 2027 elections. - Published4 days ago - Published3 days ago

Perez Hilton faces long recovery after reports he self-harmed during livestream - Published The US blogger Perez Hilton is in a "serious but stable" condition after being admitted to hospital, according to his family. Emergency services were called to his Miami home on Tuesday after members of the public reported concerns while watching a TikTok livestream. The Miami sheriff's office confirmed they attended a scene of a man "livestreaming acts of self-harm" on Tuesday. They did not confirm his name but said the man was alone in the house at the time. A statement released on the 48-year-old's website said he "experienced significant blood loss" and his treatment and recovery would be a "long process". - If you are affected by any of the issues in this story, help and support is available at BBC Action Line. The statement, external said Hilton was being held in hospital under Florida's Baker Act, which focuses on providing services for people experiencing a mental health crisis. The father-of-three, whose real name is Mario Lavandeira, is expected to have surgery in the coming days. A TikTok spokesman said its automated moderation systems flagged the livestream to the company's US moderation team for review within minutes. A moderator error caused a delay in the removal, TikTok said, but the company alerted law enforcement to the situation, closed several subsequent streams within 90 seconds, and banned the account. The pseudonym Perez Hilton is a reference to Paris Hilton, who was at the height of her fame when the celebrity gossip blog was launched in 2005. The website would go on to attract eight million hits a day at a time when the internet was still in its relative infancy. It was criticised for vicious commentary of stars including Miley Cyrus and Lady Gaga. In later years, Hilton admitted having regrets about being "mean or cruel". He has also appeared on reality TV shows including Celebrity Rap Superstar and Celebrity Big Brother.

item.title: Puerto Rico rations water supplies due to intense drought
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqlxgk7r2vwo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Puerto Rico rations water supplies due to intense drought - Published Hundreds of thousands of people are going without running water for two days at a time in Puerto Rico, as authorities in the US territory take drastic measures to combat a severe drought. Many households on the Caribbean island have been split into two groups - with each having their water supply shut off for 48 hours on a rotating basis. Residents in the capital, San Juan, where the taps were turned off on Friday, decried the rationing. Officials have not said when the measure will end. Most of Puerto Rico is facing moderate to severe drought conditions, according to the US Drought Monitor, which has been compounded by long-term issues with the island's infrastructure. Puerto Rico's water authority says about 65% of the water it produces is lost or goes unbilled, much of it through leaks and ageing pipes, according to the BBC's US news partner CBS. The island's Governor Jenniffer González has acknowledged these issues, but says rationing was implemented due to the weather, which has left the crucial Carraízo reservoir depleted. Puerto Rico experienced its driest July on record, with 68% of the island currently facing drought conditions. Seven regions usually served by the reservoir have been affected, with 180,000 properties subject to rationing, the government said. González said the decision was taken "after carefully evaluating the current conditions of the Carraízo reservoir in conjunction with weather forecasts". "This situation is beyond our control," she said in a statement. "It is the result of the weather conditions we have been facing, which experts had warned about weeks ago." As the mains outages take effect, people have been queuing at water tanker trucks sent to affected regions to fill up large bottles. "It's unbelievable to live through this today," San Juan resident Gloriany Baba told CBS, describing the conditions as "brutal". But there is some confusion in the territory as to which households and businesses will be affected and when. The Morcelo area, south of San Juan, was promised water on Friday, with the supply set to be shut off on Sunday, after the first 48-hour period had ended. But residents have told local media that running water was not available. "People are uncertain because they know we're in the 48-hour window where we're supposed to have drinking water," community leader Rubén Torres told newspaper El Nuevo Dia on Saturday. "What's happening? The first 24 hours have already passed and the water hasn't arrived." As well as degraded infrastructure and a lack of rain, experts have also pointed to too much sediment in resevoirs as a factor in the water crisis. Water rationing measures have been tried previously in 2020 and 2015, when some 400,000 households only received running water every third day. Puerto Rico has previously been shaken by the kind of extreme weather events scientists say are more likely due to human-induced climate change. The island's electricity grid was devastated in 2017 by Hurricane Maria, which caused thousands of deaths. Scientists say the extreme amounts of rainfall it brought was made more likely due to climate change. González also told CNN there were more than 1,000 wildfires currently burning in Puerto Rico, and that rain could return when a cloud of Saharan dust drifts away from the Caribbean. "It's a difficult situation," she said, adding that the US federal government was "helping us out", without elaborating. BBC News has approached the US disaster agency Fema for comment. item.title: An unbearable rotting stench is plaguing an LA neighbourhood
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c2elpz33zp2o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
An unbearable rotting stench is plaguing an LA neighbourhood - Published On any typical day, Alexis Sicairos and his girlfriend have a line of patrons waiting to order a banana buzz latte or a cloud matcha at their Los Angeles coffee stand. But now, the street corner where they sit is largely empty. The reason is clear the second you walk into the neighbourhood: it stinks. On 17 June, a fire destroyed a large cold-storage warehouse in the area, leaving behind some 85 million lb (39 million kg) of rotting food, including beef, pork, poultry and seafood. Nearly two months later, residents of Boyle Heights say the clean-up has taken a lot longer than expected and they've grown frustrated with the pungent odour hovering over the area. "It smells really bad, like really bad... to the point that you want to throw up," says Mesha, a 37-year-old security guard stationed outside a marijuana dispensary. She likens the smell to that of a dead body. Lineage, the company that operated the warehouse, said that as of Monday about 80% of the food waste had been removed. But city officials said this week that the company's response had "fallen short" and that they have issued public health and safety violation notices. "It's been tough," Sicairos, 30, says. After shutting down his coffee stand for two weeks because of the fire, Brew Sting has reopened - but the demand hasn't been the same. He says flies have been swarming relentlessly over the past weeks, since the food that was stored in the warehouse began rotting. The warehouse workers that would previously line up to buy coffee haven't been showing up over the past two months. "Due to the fire, obviously most of them aren't here," Sicairos says. "So we lost those customers, but we also lost customers that don't want to be around the smell, the smoke, the flies. It's understandable. But we have to keep paying our bills, so we're still here." One cannot walk through the area, which is mostly a warehouse district surrounded by homes, without swatting away countless flies, both big and small, including black, blue and green ones. As Sicairos packs up his coffee stand for the day, flies are landing on his tables and his body. He acknowledges that patrons don't want to see flies when they're purchasing food or drinks to consume. A city-commissioned inspection report found that waste and high temperatures at the warehouse could speed up the breeding of flies capable of infecting wounds in both people and animals, a local NBC affiliate reported, external. The report from a pest control company said it could put people and animals with open wounds at risk of contracting disease. People in the community have also reported seeing large rats, and they say traps placed along sidewalks aren't big enough to hold them. Many residents blame the city for what they deem an inadequate response to the fire and a lack of transparency and resources. "I understand why residents are frustrated," Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass told the BBC in a statement. "They deserve transparency, clear communication, and meaningful support. Since day one, I have been in Boyle Heights listening to residents, meeting with families, and making sure their voices guide our response." The mayor, who is up for re-election this year, said she directed city departments to work with local, state, federal, nonprofit and community partners to deliver immediate support and solutions. Bass has also issued executive orders to mobilise resources and speed up the cleaning process. The city says they and other local partners have brought mobile health clinics to the neighbourhood and delivered thousands of air purifiers. Late last month, the county's public health department fined Lineage for "unsanitary and nuisance" conditions with $500-a-day citations. The mayor has given Lineage a 13 August deadline to complete the cleanup. The company said on Monday that it was 80% of the way there - up from 60% on 31 July. "Our goal is to complete bulk food waste removal from the site next week," a Lineage spokesperson told the BBC on Wednesday. It expects to spend $80m-$100m (£59m-£74m) on the cleanup. Outside the warehouse, dozens of workers in hard hats and neon vests can be seen tackling the effort, some wearing face coverings. Officials with the local air quality authority and sheriff's office were also on-site. But Bass criticised the company's efforts in a letter to Lineage shareholders on Tuesday. "Residents, public agencies and elected officials have repeatedly sought timely information regarding the cleanup, remediation, environmental monitoring and recovery," she wrote. "Too often, those requests have been met with delayed communication, limited transparency, and insufficient public engagement." The mayor also directed city departments to halt plans to rebuild the warehouse "until the health and safety of the community are protected". Lineage, which is a temperature-controlled warehousing and logistics company, says "cleanup crews are working around the clock to remove food waste, clear debris and dismantle damaged sections of the structure. "However, this is a highly complex operation," they say, adding that reducing odours is a "key priority" in their cleanup effort. Related topics - Published22 June - Published17 July

item.title: Israel accused of weaponising archaeology at ancient West Bank sites
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c20d8qre98do?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Israel accused of weaponising archaeology at ancient West Bank sites - Published Up in the hills above the Roman columns of the ancient site of Sebastia, in the occupied West Bank, are olive fields that have been cultivated for generations by Palestinian families. One of the landowners, Abu Mudif, says he has received notification that his land is part of a tranche of about 450 acres that the Israeli authorities are taking possession of in order, they say, to protect and develop the site for a major new national park. Typically, Palestinian landowners receive little or no payment for such land expropriation. And even when it is offered, most refuse it as they see accepting it as giving recognition and legitimacy to the loss of what they see as their patrimony. It's a vital income for Abu Mudif to lose of course, but it goes deeper than that for him. "If I wanted to describe it, the closest description I can give is that it is like having your soul ripped away. I cannot imagine myself without my land." Nahed Sakha owns a local restaurant that is under threat of demolition. He says the Israeli plan seems to be to cut Palestinian residents off from the archaeological site, which dates back thousands of years and has significant remains from the ancient Jewish past, as well as many other eras including the Romans, the Crusaders and the Ottomans. "Restoration work has now begun along with excavations," he says. "Landowners were told that no-one would be allowed to use or plough their land." The concerns of the village that surrounds Sebastia have been echoed by the United Nations culture and education agency, Unesco, which has now declared it not just a World Heritage Site but also added it to the List of World Heritage in Danger. Unesco says that the main threat facing the site concerns what it calls the "planned expropriation and creation of the 'Samaria' (Shomron) national park, which could divide the property". Standing on a path between the entrance car park in Sebastia on one side - where the Roman-era forum once stood - and the columns of the basilica on the other, the village mayor, Mohammed Azem, looks down to his right at some rubbish left in the ruins. He says locals are now worried about reaching down to clean the area as it might cause problems with Israeli security forces and settlers. The path on which he stands divides the site between Area B of the West Bank - which is under Palestinian civil and Israeli security control - and Area C, which is under full Israeli civil and security control. Last week, Israel allocated roughly 113 million shekels (£27.8m), external to expanding its control over archaeological sites in the West Bank. Some projects involve sites in areas administered by the Palestinian Authority. In the remains of the Roman theatre, Israeli activist Alon Arad - who heads Emek Shaveh, an Israeli group that aims to ensure that the ancient heritage of the region belongs to all communities - says that the Israeli authorities have bypassed consultation with the local administration and residents of Sebastia. "The thing is that Israel is not the owner of this place. This is a Palestinian heritage site. And in order to develop it in a positive way, it has to be done with the local community, with the municipality, so they can benefit." The Israeli plans would see Sebastia's entrance moved to the other side of the vast site, away from the village and current car park and shops. The Palestinian tourism and foreign ministries have expressed their hope that recognition by Unesco may buttress international support for their opposition to Israeli land seizures in Sebastia. But the Israeli Foreign Minister, Gideon Saar, has portrayed Unesco's move as enabling Palestinian efforts to diminish historic Jewish ties to the West Bank. "No vote in an international organisation can change history," he asserted. Further to the south in the West Bank and just in sight of Jerusalem is Herodium, a manmade hill with an extraordinary palace built on its summit by King Herod, who ruled the Kingdom of Judea just before the Christian era. Recently here, too, Israel has begun to expropriate land - this time about 80 acres - for what it says is the "preservation and development" of the site. Peace Now - an Israeli organisation that monitors settlements - says: "Under international law, as well as according to rulings of the Israeli Supreme Court, Israel is prohibited from expropriating land for settlement purposes or exclusively for the benefit of Israeli citizens". "Consequently, in order for the expropriation to be considered lawful, the state will likely argue that the site is intended to serve both Palestinian and Israeli populations, despite the apparent fact that its primary rationale and purpose are linked to settlement expansion and Israeli control." For Shmuel Browns, who has worked on excavations in Herodium and leads deeply enthused guided tours, it's vital for Israeli archaeologists and officials to be able to oversee and protect places that are so freighted with historical and religious significance. "Israel feels responsible to look after the archaeology, the artifacts, the history of this land," he says. But there has also been a drive to go further than this among far-right members of Israel's current government. A new law was proposed earlier this year that would have transferred control of archaeological sites to the Israeli heritage ministry from the Civil Administration, which operates under military authority, and given it sweeping powers to seize land for archaeological preservation across the West Bank. That bill passed its first reading in parliament in May but is now on hold as elections are coming up. It may never re-emerge. Back in Sebastia, the Israeli activist Alon Arad says the very fact that the bill was put forward shows how archaeology itself has been weaponised in the West Bank. "This is exactly how the mechanism works. You use archaeology, you use it in order to do excavations and to the narrative, to rewrite history, but you also use it in order to allocate lands or reallocate lands from Palestinian to Israeli," he warns. Increasingly, Palestinian residents of Sebastia fear that their close connection with the ruins is in danger of being lost.

Man arrested after boat capsizes near Statue of Liberty killing woman and infant - Published The operator of a boat that overturned near the Statue of Liberty, killing a woman and a baby, has been arrested and charged with reckless endangerment, New York police said. Officials said a large search and rescue operation was launched after the incident near New York Harbour on Saturday night. Twelve people who were initially rescued from the water are all reported to be in stable condition. New York police divers later found a 27-year-old woman and a five-month-old girl, who were transported to a nearby hospital where they later died. The names of passengers and the specific cause of the incident have not been released by officials. Around 22:25 local time (03:25 BST), police received a 911 call reporting an overturned boat in the waters near Liberty Island, which houses the iconic statue. A nearby tour operator Sea the City saw the capsized boat and helped pull 11 people from the water, the company's founder Adam Schwartz said according to the BBC's US partner CBS News. The rescue involved two Coast Guard boats, four fire department boats, two police boats and a police helicopter, the USCG said. The investigation into the incident is ongoing, officials said. The boat's operator, a 46-year-old Manhattan resident, faces 13 counts of reckless endangerment, officials said. Coast Guard investigators are also determining whether the boat was illegally chartered. An illegal charter is any passenger-for-hire vessel operation that does not have required credentials, safety equipment, and certificate of inspection. "We are extremely grateful for the heroic, swift actions of our partner agencies and Good Samaritan vessel who assisted in rescuing survivors from the water," said Capt Doreen McCarthy of the USCG.

item.title: Hormuz talks positive, Oman says, as Iran warns deal would not open strait
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c934j5y2lq9o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Hormuz talks positive, Oman says, as Iran warns deal would not open strait - Published Oman has said positive talks have been taking place with Iran over an agreement to secure a shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz, as Tehran warned that any deal would not see an immediate reopening of the vital waterway. Both sides suggested on Saturday that discussions were progressing, but a timeline on any deal being finalised remained unclear. Oman's foreign ministry warned against attacks on shipping that could hamper that. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said talks were in their final stages but the reopening of the strait remained "subject to other conditions". Tehran has effectively blockaded the waterway, through which around a fifth of the world's oil and natural gas usually flows, since the US and Israel began attacking it in February. Talks in recent days have focused on the possibility of a deal between Iran and Oman on a new route through the strait, which they would both have responsibility for and is hoped would lead to progress in resuming shipping traffic. But Araghchi said a full reopening of the typically busy maritime route depended on other conditions being met, of which he provided a cursory appraisal. He said the conditions included Iran receiving compensation from the US for what Tehran described as violations of the deal both sides signed in June to cease fighting and advance talks to end the war. That deal - called a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) - quickly fell through, as did diplomatic talks, with tit-for-tat attacks resuming just days after it was signed. Separately, Mohammad Baqer Zolqadr, Iran's security chief, told the semi-official news agency Tasnim that the Strait of Hormuz would not reopen until the US "corrects" its behaviour. He said the US needed to meet six Iranian demands, including a halt to threats against Iran, removal of its naval blockade of Iranian ports and release of Iran's frozen assets. Another blockade, on Saudi Arabia's ports in the Red Sea, had been imposed by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis since 20 July. Earlier this week, US President Donald Trump said a deal with Iran "could be soon", but Vice-President JD Vance appeared to be more sceptical on Saturday, telling Fox News that work remained to be done even if progress was being made. "We're really in the middle of the game here," he said. "This thing is not over." Vance added that "we're applying a whole host of tools - diplomatic, economic [and] military tools - to ensure that we get the best outcome for the American people". Additionally, he claimed that the "same amount of oil" will emerge from the Gulf as did before the US military operation began on 28 February, although he offered no details. "What we're really working through now is how you can actually set up a traffic scheme so that the ships can pass through safely," he added. One of the main points of disagreement between Tehran and Washington has been Iran's reported threat to impose a fee on vessels wishing to cross the strait. Reuters - citing an Iranian official - previously reported that Tehran was seeking fees of between 5% and 7% of the price of cargoes from vessels who travel through it. Vance downplayed those reports, saying: "The Iranians have told us they have no plans to toll the Strait of Hormuz." Oman's warning against attacks on ships in the strait came as the United Arab Emirates (UAE) said on Saturday that Iran had targeted a tanker affiliated with Adnoc, its state-owned oil company, as it passed through. The UAE's foreign ministry said in a statement that a "hostile Iranian attack" had hit an Adnoc tanker "with a missile". It added that there were no casualties. Later on Saturday, the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency also reported a ship being struck by "an unknown projectile" off the coast of Oman, causing "a fire that has been extinguished" but no casualties. It is unclear whether UKMTO was referring to the same ship as the UAE. Related topics - Published4 days ago - Published5 days ago

item.title: Spain imposes border controls against Italy as row over Ceuta migrant influx intensifies
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5yv5l6yr5ko?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Spain imposes border controls against Italy as row over Ceuta migrant influx intensifies - Published Spain has imposed border controls on all air and sea travel from Italy as a row between the two EU countries intensifies. The measures - which started at midnight (22:00 GMT) and will last for a month - come a week after Italy introduced similar restrictions following an influx of about 78,000 migrants from Morocco into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta. Spanish officials said the documents of 5%-10% of passengers were being checked before they were allowed to disembark planes. Italy has also said its border controls are random. The crisis has pitted Spain's socialist leader Pedro Sanchez against Italy's conservative leader Giorgia Meloni - who has long called for stricter EU migration rules. Italy does not share a land border with Spain. Its government said last week that decision to temporarily suspend the border-free Schengen arrangement was to prevent any of the migrants who had entered Ceuta from travelling on to Italy. Madrid dismissed this position, saying it was based on "spurious arguments" that lacked any basis in fact because the migrants who entered Ceuta had no way of entering the Schengen area. On Friday, Spain demanded Italy reverse its checks by Sunday. Rome said they would stay until at least 15 August - when, it said, Spain "expects a new wave of migration" to hit Ceuta. Italy has said that Spanish and EU citizens are exempt from additional checks when arriving in Italy, with these extra steps only for non-EU residents. However, it is not clear how border officials were meant to distinguish between EU and non-EU travellers and El Pais has reported that several Italian airport terminals have seen long queues and waiting times in recent days, with passengers arriving from Spain directed to a specific line for checks. As for Spanish controls, the authorities insists the immigration checks are random. However, a passenger arriving in Madrid on Saturday told national broadcaster RTVE that all passengers on her flight had had to show their passports. "They told us we couldn't get off the plane without showing our documents," Elisa said. Another passenger said "we were stopped and asked for identification, which the police seemed to approve of". Spain says its checks will stay in place until 7 September "unless a change in the circumstances that led to its adoption warrants modifying that period". Temporary suspensions of the Schengen agreement are not unprecedented. Italy also maintains controls on its border with Slovenia. Italy's decision to suspend Schengen for a month was backed by Finland and Denmark, while the Czech Republic called for Spain's membership to be temporarily suspended. Most of the migrants who arrived in Ceuta last week were returned within days. One hundred are believed to have died during the crossing. Nearly 1,400 minors, some of them "very young boys and girls", still remain there. Spain has not announced an anticipated second wave of crossings from Morocco. But BBC Arabic has found dozens of Facebook posts calling for a second crossing in mid-August, including some that advertised swimming equipment for sale. Six of these groups had more than 100,000 followers. Meta says it has removed posts that violate its policy. The Spanish prime minister's office told El Pais they were monitoring the situation but did not expect a repeat of scenes from last week. It remains unclear exactly why tens of thousands of migrants attempted to cross into Ceuta, but the EU's Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner has suggested criminal networks spreading disinformation were to blame - an assertion the Spanish government has agreed with. The crossings came after Spain's Supreme Court ruled that migrants stopped at sea while trying to reach Ceuta or Melilla cannot be summarily returned to Morocco. Morocco, for its part, has laid blame for the crisis on the court, with an unnamed government source briefing local outlets that "the deterrent element of the system collapsed and the dam gave way, not under the weight of the criminals, but of a judge's decision". The number of people swimming to Ceuta at once has raised questions about why Morocco's border guards did not attempt to stop them. The two exclaves have long been a bone of diplomatic contention between Spain and Morocco, which does not recognise Spanish sovereignty over them. item.title: Child among three killed in Russian missile attacks near Kyiv
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cz7dy8gq99eo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Child among three killed in Russian missile attacks near Kyiv - Published At least three people, including a child, have been killed in overnight Russian attacks near the Ukrainian capital Kyiv, a local official said. Another three people were injured as ballistic missiles hit east of Kyiv, head of the regional military administration Timur The new attack comes just days after 21 people were killed as Russia intensifies its strikes, aware that Ukraine has been running out of Western-donated interceptor missiles used to defend its skies. On Saturday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky issued a fresh call for more US-made Patriot interceptor missiles, saying what his country was receiving was not enough. Zelensky's plea comes days after US President Donald Trump appeared to go back on a promise to grant Ukraine a licence to manufacture the defensive systems. On Saturday, Ukraine's president still referred to an agreement with the US on a licence. Since coming to office, Trump has scaled back direct military aid for Ukraine. Instead, Ukraine's European allies have been buying expensive US supplies - such as Patriot missiles - which are then donated to Ukraine. "Ukraine does not have, nor will it ever have, the sort of funds that Russia has, which it is using to finance the war," Zelensky said on Saturday. "We have what we need, thanks to European aid and support from other countries. But additional funding specifically for Ukrainian production is what is needed." Earlier in the week, Zelensky said the supply of interceptors from allies had been "significantly reduced" this year. The Ukrainian leader was speaking during his first trip to Serbia. He met President Aleksandar Vučić to discuss economic ties, security issues and relations with the European Union. Zelensky is trying to build wider support for Ukraine, but Vučić, a close ally of Russian President Vladimir Putin, has refused to impose sanctions on Russia. Serbia is trying to join the EU and has provided aid to Ukraine and promised to help it rebuild after the war. At the joint news conference with Zelensky in the capital, Belgrade, Vučić focused on Ukraine's European accession and pledged to support it. Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Since then, Russia has seized parts of Ukraine in the east, but the front lines have remained unchanged for a long time. Trump's efforts to mediate an end to the conflict have faltered recently, leading to an escalation of attacks between the two warring sides. Ukraine has developed advanced drones able to hit deep into Russian territory in an effort to take the war to Russia. In the latest such attack, the Ukrainian military hit Russia's Ilsky and Syzran oil refineries during overnight attacks, causing fires at both, the Ukrainian general staff said on Saturday. Moscow-linked vessels in the Black Sea were also hit - according to Zelensky the intention is to limit oil revenues used by Russia to "finance" its war. The Russia-Ukraine war has threatened to spill over into neighbouring countries. There have been several instances of drones or missiles flying into their territories. On most occasions, Russia has been blamed, but denied any involvement. On Saturday, a drone entered Bulgarian airspace and exploded near an international gas pipeline, its prime minister said, after crossing from Romania. Rumen Radev said it had been carrying a "significant" amount of explosives but there had been no casualties or reports of damage. Bulgaria's defence ministry said it appeared to be a Maya decoy drone, which is known to be used by Ukraine. "At the moment, there is no reason to believe that the incident was intentional," the ministry said. Later, Heorhii Tykhyi, spokesman for Ukraine's foreign ministry, was quoted as saying that "we can say with certainty that the Ukrainian Armed Forces did not intentionally direct any assets toward Bulgaria", but stopped short of admitting the drone was Ukrainian.
